سلامت زیر تیغ تورم و ناکارآمدی بیمه‌ها؛ بازنشستگان درمان خود را به تعویق می‌اندازند

source.author: رضا اکوانیان

claim.statement: On 29 April 2026, ILNA published direct accounts from low-income workers and retirees in Tehran, Rasht, and Sanandaj showing treatment triage: a service worker said metformin rose from 170,000 to 450,000-500,000 toman and she paid 13 million toman upfront for several months of medicine despite a 20 million toman salary and 10 million toman rent; a retired heart patient said he could not afford Plavix and stretched specialist visits; and a private-school teacher with thyroid cancer said each two-week prescription rose from 300,000 to 900,000 toman while tests cost 3 million every 45 days and insurance paid about 10%.
claim.subject: Iranian low-income workers and retirees with chronic illness
claim.object: medicine rationing, skipped care, and large out-of-pocket payments

evidence.summary: ILNA reported named worker/retiree cases from Tehran, Rasht, and Sanandaj, with medication price jumps, skipped Plavix, delayed specialist visits, 13M upfront medicine spending, and insurance covering only about 10% of some test costs.

information_depth.rationale: Direct Persian labor-source reporting includes city, condition, medication names, income, rent, price changes, and insurance details.

claim.statement: On 20 April 2026, ILNA reported that Salman Eshaghi, spokesman for parliament's Health and Treatment Commission, said the commission had reviewed price increases for some medicines caused by coordination failures among agencies; he acknowledged that in some cases patients' payment shares had risen and caused dissatisfaction, while claiming subsequent insurance-system corrections had improved the situation and that hard-to-treat disease medicines were covered at 90-95%.
claim.subject: Iran parliament health commission
claim.object: drug price and patient co-pay disruptions

evidence.summary: ILNA quoted Salman Eshaghi describing committee review of medicine price rises, patient co-pay increases, insurance correction measures, and claimed 90-95% coverage for hard-to-treat disease medicines.

information_depth.rationale: The official statement confirms administrative disruption and patient-payment effects but the claimed fixes need independent verification.

assessment.uncertainty: Government claims that corrections largely resolved the issue are not independently verified by the same source.

claim.statement: On 19 April 2026, Iran International reported Saeed Fatahi of the Supreme Center of Iranian Workers' Guild Associations warning that treatment and drug costs had risen sharply after the war, dental care had become a luxury for retirees, many retirees were forced to defer treatment or forgo necessary services, and some borrowed money or sold small assets to pay for care; the same report cited ILNA that insured patients still pay significant costs despite the legal promise of free Social Security treatment and may wait months for partial supplemental-insurance reimbursement.
claim.subject: Iranian retirees
claim.object: treatment because insurance and income do not cover health costs

evidence.summary: The report quoted Saeed Fatahi on drug/treatment costs, dental care as luxury, deferred care, borrowing/selling assets, and cited ILNA on out-of-pocket payments and delayed supplemental-insurance reimbursements.

information_depth.rationale: Named labor adviser, explicit mechanisms of deferred care, insurance gaps, and household coping behavior are reported.

claim.statement: On 30 April 2026, Iran International reported that war and economic crisis had deepened worker unemployment and health risk: it cited Etemad estimates of more than one million jobs lost and two million direct or indirect unemployed, Labor Minister Ahmad Meydari saying 147,000 people registered for unemployment insurance in two months, Ali Khodaei warning unemployment insurance covers less than half household costs, and construction-sector figures of 1.5-1.7 million workers with about half lacking Social Security coverage; the article linked this pressure to food insecurity and treatment deferral.
claim.subject: Iranian workers
claim.object: post-war unemployment, weak safety nets, and treatment/food insecurity

evidence.summary: The May Day article reported job-loss estimates, unemployment-insurance registrations, weak insurance replacement, construction-worker insurance gaps, and links to inability to pay food, rent, and treatment.

information_depth.rationale: Concrete job-loss, registration, sector, and health-risk figures are given, but some unemployment estimates are attributed indirectly.

question.text: Can treatment deferral and skipped essential medicines be quantified through pharmacy, hospital, insurer, or patient-association data rather than anecdotal reporting?
question.why_it_matters: Quantifying skipped care would show whether the health-access crack is isolated pain or a population-scale mortality risk.

operations.rationale: Direct worker/patient stories show how the documented medicine repricing appears as rationing, skipped medicines, and major out-of-pocket spending.
The ILNA cases include diabetes medicine and insulin scarcity, corroborating patient-level insulin access stress.
The official co-pay/coverage-disruption statement gives institutional context for rare-disease insurance warnings.
Both claims show retirees translating insurance failure and medicine/treatment costs into postponed care and protest pressure.
Unemployment, weak unemployment insurance, and lack of Social Security coverage compound the minimum-wage purchasing-power collapse.
The broader post-war unemployment article provides context for factory damage, layoffs, and wage-arrears evidence.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v8 — skipped care becomes worker survival signal
synthesis.summary: The eighth pass moves the health-access thread from institutional warning to lived triage. Direct ILNA reporting has workers and retirees naming exact medicines, cities, incomes, rent, and coping behavior: metformin roughly tripled, insulin is hard to find, a Tehran service worker paid 13M toman upfront for medicine against a 20M salary and 10M rent, a Rasht heart patient cannot afford Plavix and stretches specialist visits, and a Sanandaj teacher with cancer says insurance covers only about 10% of tests. This is reinforced by an Apr 19 retiree-care report: dental care is now described as a luxury, retirees defer treatment or skip services, and supplemental insurance reimbursement can be delayed for months. The state has noticed the pressure: ILNA quoted parliament's health-commission spokesman acknowledging drug price and patient co-pay disruption from coordination failures, even while claiming fixes. On the labor side, the May Day unemployment article adds the safety-net context: over 1M jobs estimated lost, 147k unemployment-insurance registrations in two months, and many construction workers uninsured. Net: the crack is now treatment triage under wage collapse, not just medicine inflation.
synthesis.limitations: The strongest skipped-care evidence is still qualitative, based on direct cases and named institutional warnings rather than population-scale pharmacy or insurer data. The parliamentary statement claims fixes and high hard-to-treat drug coverage, but that claim is not independently verified. xPool May Day results did not add reliable inside-Iran protest evidence in this pass.

information_depth.rationale: Direct ILNA patient narratives, named labor-adviser warning, official parliamentary statement, and May Day unemployment data converge on treatment triage under wage collapse.

operations.reason: v8 adds direct patient/worker treatment-triage evidence, official drug co-pay disruption acknowledgement, retiree treatment deferral, and May Day unemployment/safety-net context.
